In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[topology]], a '''regular homotopy''' refers to a special kind of [[homotopy]] between [[immersion (mathematics)|immersion]]s of one [[manifold]] in another. The homotopy must be a 1-parameter family of immersions.

Similar to [[homotopy class]]es, one defines two immersions to be in the same regular homotopy class if there exists a regular homotopy between them. Regular homotopy for immersions is similar to [[Homotopy#Isotopy|isotopy]] of embeddings: they are both restricted types of homotopies.  Stated another way, two continuous functions <math>f,g : M \to N</math> are homotopic if they represent points in the same path-components of the mapping space <math>C(M, N)</math>, given the [[compact-open topology]]. The '''space of immersions''' is the subset of <math>C(M, N)</math> consisting of immersions, denoted by <math>\operatorname{Imm}(M, N)</math>, given the <math> C^1 </math> topology. Two immersions <math>f, g: M \to N</math> are '''regularly homotopic''' if they represent points in the same path-component of <math>\operatorname{Imm}(M,N)</math>.

== Examples ==
Any two knots in 3-space are equivalent by regular homotopy, though not by isotopy.[[File:Winding Number Around Point.svg|thumb|300px|This curve has [[total curvature]] 6''π'', and [[turning number]] 3.]]
The '''Whitney–Graustein theorem''' {{anchor|Whitney–Graustein theorem}} classifies the regular homotopy classes of a circle into the plane; two immersions are regularly homotopic if and only if they have the same [[turning number]] – equivalently, [[total curvature]]; equivalently, if and only if their [[Gauss map]]s have the same degree/[[winding number]].

[[File:MorinSurfaceFromTheTop.PNG|thumb|Smale's classification of immersions of spheres shows that [[sphere eversion]]s exist, which can be realized via this [[Morin surface]].]]
[[Stephen Smale]] classified the regular homotopy classes of a ''k''-sphere immersed in  <math>\mathbb R^n</math> – they are classified by [[homotopy groups]] of [[Stiefel manifold]]s, which is a generalization of the Gauss map, with here ''k'' partial derivatives not vanishing. More precisely, the set <math>I(n,k)</math> of regular homotopy classes of embeddings of sphere <math>S^k</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is in one-to-one correspondence with elements of group <math>\pi_k\left(V_k\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)\right)</math>. In case <math>k = n - 1</math> we have <math>V_{n-1}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right) \cong SO(n)</math>. Since <math>SO(1)</math> is path connected, <math>\pi_2(SO(3)) \cong \pi_2\left(\mathbb{R}P^3\right) \cong \pi_2\left(S^3\right) \cong 0</math> and <math>\pi_6(SO(6)) \to \pi_6(SO(7)) \to \pi_6\left(S^6\right) \to \pi_5(SO(6)) \to \pi_5(SO(7))</math> and due to [[Bott periodicity theorem]] we have <math>\pi_6(SO(6))\cong \pi_6(\operatorname{Spin}(6))\cong \pi_6(SU(4))\cong \pi_6(U(4)) \cong 0</math> and since <math>\pi_5(SO(6)) \cong \mathbb{Z},\  \pi_5(SO(7)) \cong 0</math> then we have <math>\pi_6(SO(7))\cong 0</math>. Therefore all immersions of spheres <math>S^0,\ S^2</math> and <math>S^6</math> in euclidean spaces of one more dimension are regular homotopic. In particular, spheres <math>S^n</math> embedded in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math> admit [[sphere eversion|eversion]] if <math>n = 0, 2, 6</math>, i.e. one can turn these spheres "inside-out".

Both of these examples consist of reducing regular homotopy to homotopy; this has subsequently been substantially generalized in the [[homotopy principle]] (or ''h''-principle) approach.

==Non-degenerate homotopy==

For [[locally convex]], closed [[space curve]]s, one can also define non-degenerate homotopy. Here, the 1-parameter family of immersions must be non-degenerate (i.e. the curvature may never vanish). There are 2 distinct non-degenerate homotopy classes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Feldman|first=E. A.|date=1968|title=Deformations of closed space curves|journal=Journal of Differential Geometry|language=en|volume=2|issue=1|pages=67–75|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214501138 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Further restrictions of non-vanishing torsion lead to 4 distinct equivalence classes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Little|first=John A.|date=1971|title=Third order nondegenerate homotopies of space curves|journal=Journal of Differential Geometry|language=en|volume=5|issue=3|pages=503–515|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214430012 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
